# Preface: How to Use This Book {.unnumbered epub:type=preface}

This book teaches a way of publishing in which you write once, in plain text, and every
output rebuilds itself from that one source: a web page, a Word document, a PDF, slides, an
e-book, a website, a blog and a dashboard. A coding assistant writes most of the code; you
decide what to build, check what it wrote, and remain responsible for the result. The tool
that turns the sources into outputs is Quarto, which is free and open source.

It grew out of a one-day workshop, and it keeps the workshop's shape: two real projects, built
step by step, with a way to catch up from any point. It also explains what the workshop only
had time to show: why each step works, where it fails, and when not to take it.

## Who this book is for {.unnumbered}

Researchers, analysts, students and anyone else who writes documents from data and is new to
Quarto, to coding assistants or to both. Many readers will have little experience with a
terminal, and Chapter 3 teaches the little you need. No programming is assumed: the book
explains the Python the assistant writes, but you will not have to write it yourself.

You will need a computer on which you can install software (Windows, Mac or Linux), a free
GitHub account, and access to one coding assistant, which requires a paid plan or an API key.

## The two running examples {.unnumbered}

Every concept is tied to one of two projects, both built on real, cited data.

**A London visitor guide** (Part II). You work for the city's tourism office and write one
guide that becomes a web page, a Word brief for partners, a printed flyer, a dashboard for
managers and a published website, with every visitor number computed from the Association of
Leading Visitor Attractions' published counts.

**Drinking-water risk in Colombian municipalities** (Part III). You group Colombia's
municipal zones into kinds by water safety, services and context, compare health and
education outcomes between the kinds, and publish the analysis as a report, slides, a blog
post and a website, all from one analysis script. The data are Colombian open data, joined
by official municipality codes.

## How the book is organised {.unnumbered}

**Part I** covers what you need before the first project: what Quarto does (@sec-quarto),
how to work with a coding assistant safely (@sec-assistant) and how to set up your computer
(@sec-setup). **Part II** builds the London guide, from a first Markdown file to a published
website, and ends by changing an input and explaining what the rebuild changed. **Part III**
does the same for the water analysis, with the statistics explained on the way: exploring
data, preparing features, clustering with k-means, interpreting the clusters and resisting a
causal reading of them. The appendices hold the Windows setup, a cheatsheet, troubleshooting,
every checkpoint, the data sources and an account of how this book itself is built.

## How the hands-on parts work {.unnumbered}

Hands-on steps use a three-part box, explained in @sec-boxes: the exact prompt to give your
assistant, what it will probably run, and the few things only you can do. Prompts are
examples, not transcripts: assistants vary, so check the result rather than the wording.

Four kinds of aside appear throughout:

::: why
**Why this works** explains the mechanism behind a step.
:::

::: pitfall
**Common pitfall** describes a failure seen in practice, and how to avoid it.
:::

::: practice
**In practice** gives a judgement call or a habit, and the occasional question to pause on.
:::

::: tryit
**Try it** is an exercise, ending with the check that tells you it worked.

::: done
you can tell the four asides apart.
:::
:::

Steps marked *optional* are extensions for readers who are ahead; nothing later depends on
them.

## Two ways through {.unnumbered}

**Self-paced.** Read in order. Chapters 2 and 3 can be done in one sitting before you start
Part II; each later chapter ends at a checkpoint, so you can stop there and resume later.

**Workshop-paced.** The book follows the six-hour workshop it came from (with two 15-minute
breaks and a 30-minute meal). In the workshop, Chapter 3 and the reading in Chapter 2 are done
at home beforehand.

| Time | Block | Chapters |
|---|---|---|
| before the day | Setup, and reading about assistants and AI policy | 2, 3 |
| 0:00 | Welcome, objective, outcome | Preface |
| 0:10 | What Quarto is | 1 |
| 0:15 | Ready to prompt: the boxes and prompting | 2 |
| 0:30 | London: Markdown to HTML, rules, environment | 4 |
| 1:05 | *Break* | |
| 1:20 | London: computed documents, audiences, publishing, a rebuild | 5, 6, 7 |
| 2:25 | *Meal* | |
| 2:55 | Water: question, data, explore, prepare, cluster | 8 to 11 |
| 4:20 | *Break* | |
| 4:35 | Water: interpret, correlation and causation, publish many | 12, 13, 14 |
| 5:50 | Done: show your sites | Afterword |

## When you fall behind {.unnumbered}

Every hands-on block ends at a *checkpoint*: a folder in the workshop repository
(`checkpoints/`) holding the project as it should be at that point, with a README listing the
steps to catch up. The workshop's rule is simple: **stuck for two minutes, catch up**, and
rejoin everyone at the next block. The same rule works alone. Each exercise ends with its
catch-up line, which you paste into your assistant (@fig-catch-up).

![Catching up from a checkpoint. Your work is backed up first, so nothing is lost.](media/diagrams/catch-up){#fig-catch-up .on-light fig-alt="Stuck for two minutes, you paste the line Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/NN/README.md into the assistant. It follows four steps. One, back up your project folder, all but its .venv environment, to a new time-stamped folder beside it. Two, copy the checkpoint in, and for the water project the data if they are missing. Three, render and check a named output. Four, rejoin at the next hands-on block, which the README names."}

A checkpoint holds the end of its block, so it can be ahead of the step you were on: after
catching up, skip the block's remaining prompts and read on to the next exercise. The
exercises at the end of each part, and @sec-checkpoints, list every checkpoint.

## Two editions {.unnumbered}

This book comes as an e-book (EPUB) and as a website, built from the same source. Everything
interactive runs in the website edition: three 3-D scenes you can turn with the mouse and two
data explorers with menus. The e-book shows each of them as an animation or a still picture,
with a link and a QR code to the live version. Animations play in readers that support them;
readers that do not show the first frame, which is designed to be a useful still. The website
also respects your system's reduced-motion setting.

The website edition is at <https://project-delphi.github.io/quarto-workshop/book/>.

## Versions and dates {.unnumbered}

The book was built and checked with Quarto 1.10.20 (with its bundled Typst 0.15), Python 3.12
and uv, in November 2026. Facts that change, such as the price of a model, the wording of an
assistant's screens or the limits of a free hosting plan, carry the date they were checked,
in the form "(checked 2026-11-06)". Expect some of them to have changed by the time you read
them; the principles around them should not have.
